ny_main_cliff.blurb: The main face of Shanty Cliff, set high on the right side of a drainage near Indian Lake. Mostly traditional lines with a handful of bolted routes and a few set up for top rope, running from low fifth class up through the 5.11s, with a good share of moderate climbs in the 5.6 to 5.8 range. The place is quiet and feels remote, though weekends can bring other parties. The lower part of most routes stays shaded until early afternoon, and spring runoff can leave dirt in the cracks, so a small brush helps. Most lines can be walked off or rappelled.
ny_main_cliff.parking_note: Leave the car at the Cod Pond trailhead lot on Route 8, roughly 8 miles up from the junction with Route 30.
ny_main_cliff.approach: Walk a short way up the road, drop to the river and wade across (shin to knee deep in summer), then follow the herd path up the drainage past the Slab and the Sports Arena to reach the main face on the right.

ny_black_arches_wall.blurb: A backcountry crag on Crane Mountain in the southern Adirondacks, with an east-facing wall averaging around 125 feet. The climbing is almost entirely traditional, from easy fifth class to the low 5.12s, though the bulk of it sits between 5.8 and 5.10. The cliff breaks into several sections, including an isolated buttress, a run of arching corners and a big overhang. Several sections have rappel anchors, and some need long ropes. Expect a real walk in, brushy terrain, and heavy bugs in May and June.
ny_black_arches_wall.parking_note: Drive to the end of Sky High Road, off Garnet Lake Road. The lot at the top is about 1.5 miles up a rough road, and a wrong turn is easy to make.
ny_black_arches_wall.approach: From the trailhead, head east on the Boulderwoods path and follow cairns to a fern meadow above a clear-cut. Climb the hillside past smaller cliffs, then cross a talus and brush thicket to reach the first rock, the isolated buttress.

ny_spider_s_web_the.blurb: A steep, gently overhanging cliff in Chapel Pond Pass, laced with cracks of every size, in anorthosite. Nearly everything is traditional, and the grades start at 5.8 and are concentrated in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, with a smaller group of 5.10s and a few 5.13s, so this is mainly a destination for strong climbers who like sustained, pumpy crack climbing. The wall gets plenty of sun and its steep angle lets it dry quickly. Crisp spring and fall days suit it well, and it tends to be quiet on hot days.
ny_spider_s_web_the.approach: A path leaves the road at a trailhead register, drops through woods and an open slope into a gully, then follows a faint trail up to the talus. The Web is the leftmost cliff there. Roughly 15 minutes.

ny_c_frog_s_head_the_arch.blurb: A stretch of the Trapps, the longest and most popular cliff at the Gunks, in quartz conglomerate. All traditional, and unlike the stiffer sectors the climbing here leans moderate, with most routes between 5.5 and 5.9 and just a few at 5.10 and above. Expect horizontal cracks, small roofs and plenty of exposure. Short trails marked with yellow paint lead up from the carriage road, though summer foliage can hide the right one. Spring and fall weekends bring crowds, and fall is the prime season. Grades here run stiff by reputation.

ny_6_the_good_book.blurb: The Good Book is a sector of the Books Tier at Powerlinez in Harriman State Park, the tier named after it. Walls here are short, mostly under 50 feet, with more horizontal breaks and holds than the lower tiers. The mix is traditional leads and top-rope setups, plus a few short bolted routes, from easy to the 5.11s, with most routes between 5.9 and 5.10. Rock can be gritty and sharp, and some lines have seen little traffic, so test holds. Rattlesnakes have been seen on the access trail.

ny_worthless_boulder.blurb: A small schist outcrop at the northern end of Central Park, near 110th Street, and one of the better spots for bouldering in the park. It stands around 10 feet tall but offers a good spread of wall angles, with problems from V0 up through the double digits and plenty in the V1 to V7 range. Heavy traffic has polished many footholds, so friction is poor. Bring a crash pad and a brush, check the landing for trash before pulling on, and expect curious onlookers.

ny_k_the_slime_wall.blurb: The far end of the Trapps at the Gunks, in quartz conglomerate. All traditional, and noticeably harder than most of the cliff: roughly two thirds of the routes here are 5.10 or harder, topping out in the 5.12s and a 5.13, with a smaller set of easier lines at 5.9 and below. Expect horizontal cracks, roofs and bold moves, and protection that can be sparse. The cliff sits above the carriage road, reached by short trails; weekends in spring and fall are busy, and fall is the prime season.

ny_state_brook.blurb: A newer single-pitch cliff in the town of Arietta in the southern Adirondacks, up to about 100 feet tall. Traditional climbing with bolted anchors, running from 5.6 into the low 5.11s, with most routes between 5.8 and 5.10. The variety is wide: thin faces, roofs, hand cracks, offwidths and a full-length chimney. The wall faces northwest, so it is a good pick for hot days. Some routes are still dirty, so bring a wire brush. Expect a party or two on nice weekends, and a steady uphill walk to reach it.
ny_state_brook.parking_note: Pull off on the west shoulder of Route 10, roughly 7 miles north of the Route 29A junction, across from a small driveway leading to a cabin.
ny_state_brook.approach: Follow the well-worn herd path from the road, crossing a snowmobile trail early on, and climb steadily west for a little over a mile to the left end of the cliff.

ny_main_wall.blurb: A bouldering wall in Clark Reservation State Park near Syracuse, on limestone with some shale, reaching about 17 feet in its middle section. Problems run from V0 to V7, with most between V2 and V5, so it suits beginners through solid intermediates looking for a short session away from the gym. It sits in shade and is rarely busy. Bugs can be severe in summer, so bring repellent. Stay on the established problems and paths around the wall.
ny_main_wall.parking_note: Take NY-173 east out of Syracuse; the park entrance is on the left about a mile before Jamesville. Use the main lot.
ny_main_wall.approach: From the main trailhead, a side path branches left within a minute or two and reaches the wall shortly before a bridge.

ny_i_high_e.blurb: A mid-cliff sector of the Trapps at the Gunks, in quartz conglomerate. All traditional and one to three pitches, with a broad range: a few easy lines, a lot at 5.9, and a good number of 5.10s through 5.12. Horizontal cracks, roofs and sustained exposure define it. The cliff rises above the carriage road and the approach trail leaves it through talus. Spring and fall weekends are crowded and fall is the best season. Expect stiff grades, and plan on thin protection in places.
